title: How to work a full cross-stitch
subtitle: The default stitch, taught from a single square
excerpt: A full cross-stitch is two diagonal stitches that cross at the centre of one Aida square. The lower diagonal runs bottom-left to top-right; the upper diagonal sits on top. Consistent crossing direction is what gives a finished piece its even surface.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776, cross-stitch chapter. The two-diagonal construction method described here follows the continental method documented in Weldon's Practical Needlework series (1880s), available via the Internet Archive.

glossaryTerms.definition: Two diagonal stitches worked over one Aida square, crossing at the centre to form an X. The lower diagonal is always worked first; the upper diagonal sits on top. Every stitch in a piece must cross the same way for the surface to read evenly.

A woven cotton fabric made specifically for counted cross-stitch. The threads are woven in groups to create a regular grid of holes, so the needle enters and exits at the corner of each square without splitting the weave. 14-count Aida has 14 squares per inch and is the standard beginner fabric.

A blunt-tipped needle that slips between fabric threads instead of piercing them. The blunt tip is essential for cross-stitch: it passes through the Aida holes cleanly without splitting the woven threads. Size 24 is the standard for 14-count Aida.

The six-strand embroidery thread used for cross-stitch. Each skein is made of six strands twisted together loosely; the stitcher strips out the number of strands needed for the fabric count (two strands for 14-count Aida) and threads them together.

content.text: A
full cross-stitch
is two diagonal stitches over one square of
Aida

fabric. The lower diagonal runs from bottom-left to top-right; the upper diagonal sits on top and runs from bottom-right to top-left. Working both diagonals in the same direction across every stitch in a piece is what gives the finished surface its even sheen.
For 14-count Aida, the standard starting fabric, use a size 24
tapestry needle
and two strands of
floss
stripped from a six-strand skein. The blunt tip slips through the Aida holes without splitting the weave. A sharp needle would pierce the threads and make the grid unreadable.
Working the stitch
Come up at the bottom-left hole.

The needle enters from the back of the fabric and exits through the bottom-left corner of the Aida square you are filling. Pull the thread through until a short tail sits on the back, held under the first few stitches as you work.
Go down at the top-right hole.
Push the needle down through the top-right corner of the same square. Pull through firmly but not tightly: the diagonal should sit flat against the fabric, not pucker it.
Come up at the bottom-right hole.
The needle comes up through the bottom-right corner of the same square. The first diagonal is now on the front of the fabric.
Go down at the top-left hole.
Push the needle down through the top-left corner. This second diagonal crosses over the first, forming the X. One full cross-stitch is complete.
Keeping direction consistent

The most important rule in cross-stitch is that every stitch in the piece crosses the same way. If the first diagonal in your first stitch runs bottom-left to top-right, every stitch must do the same. The second diagonal always crosses over the first in the same direction. A piece with mixed crossing directions catches the light unevenly and the surface looks patchy, even if every stitch is correctly formed.

When working a row of stitches in the same colour, many stitchers work all the lower diagonals across the row first, then come back along the row working all the upper diagonals. Both methods produce identical results. The row method is faster for long runs of the same colour; the individual method is more reliable when colour changes are frequent.
Common problems

items.symptom: The stitch looks loose or floppy on the fabric
items.cause: Tension too slack: the thread was pulled through without enough resistance.
items.fix: Pull each stitch snug enough that the X sits flat against the fabric but does not pull the Aida holes out of square. The holes should still be round when the stitch is seated.

items.symptom: The Aida holes are pulling into diamond shapes
items.cause: Tension too tight: too much force on each pull-through.
items.fix: Ease back the pull. The Aida grid should stay square. A hoop that holds the fabric taut helps maintain consistent tension without over-pulling.

items.symptom: The back of the fabric shows a tangle of thread
items.cause: The needle is not following the grid holes and is piercing the fabric threads instead.
items.fix: Check that the needle tip is passing through the corner holes of each Aida square, not through the woven threads. The tapestry needle should slip through without resistance; if it catches, move the entry point slightly.

items.symptom: The stitches cross in different directions across the piece
items.cause: The direction of the top diagonal was reversed partway through.
items.fix: Pick a direction (bottom-left to top-right for the lower diagonal, or the opposite) and mark it on the chart margin. Check every few stitches that the crossing is consistent. There is no way to fix mixed-direction stitches other than unpicking the affected area.
